title: From a question in the UI to a Codex answer
summary: Follow the question ‘Why are these lines needed?’ from a selection in the browser, through the Python server and Codex child process, and back to the Conversation tab. This walkthrough crosses four real files and returns to earlier files as calls complete. The running example selects app.js lines 114–121. Steps 10–11 describe the timeout branch; a successful request skips cleanup and continues at step 12. This is a reading walkthrough, not evidence that a live model call was made.

files.content:
cw Code Walk
STEPS
Glossary

Code Walk

INTRODUCTION

    Drag across lines to select · Shift-click to extend

    Inputs, outputs & things to know
    Questions about this code

    What would you like to understand?

    Ask about the current step or select lines in the code.

    Context: current step
    Codex · read-only

steps.title: Start at the question box
steps.explanation:
The HTML provides a context label, a question textarea, and the Ask button inside a form. Imagine typing ‘Why are these lines needed?’ after selecting some code.

The form has the ID `chat-form`. In the next file, JavaScript connects this form to the `ask` handler with `$('chat-form').onsubmit = ask`. The markup defines the controls; JavaScript supplies their behavior.
steps.inputs: Your question and the code selection already held in browser state.
steps.outputs: A form submission handled by app.js.
steps.watch_for: The textarea is required and has an 8,000-character limit. These browser checks are supplemented by server-side validation.

steps.title: Track the lines you drag over
steps.explanation:
Before submitting, you can press on a source line and drag. Pointer-down identifies the first line, records its number as an anchor, and captures the pointer so movement can continue to be tracked outside that row.

For our example, start on line 114 and drag to line 121. Pointer movement calls `extendLineDrag`, which converts the pointer position into a line number and calls `selectLines`. Pointer-up finishes the drag and focuses the question box. Shift-click can reuse the previous anchor.
steps.inputs: Pointer position, the row's data-line attribute, and an optional previous anchor.
steps.outputs: Repeated calls to selectLines with the anchor and current endpoint.
steps.watch_for: This drag handler excludes touch input to preserve native touch scrolling. A separate click handler supports single-line touch taps.

steps.title: Turn two endpoints into one range
steps.explanation:
`selectLines(114, 121)` stores `{start: 114, end: 121, anchor: 114}` in browser state. Using min and max means dragging upward works too: `selectLines(121, 114)` still selects the inclusive range 114–121, while preserving 121 as the anchor.

Every row inside that range gets the `selected` CSS class. `updateContext` then updates the labels. No request is sent yet; the selection waits in browser memory until you ask a question.
steps.inputs: An anchor line and a current endpoint, in either order.
steps.outputs: A normalized range in state.selection and highlighted code rows.
steps.watch_for: There is one contiguous selection in one file. Changing the source file or navigating to a different step clears it.

steps.title: Package the question and its context
steps.explanation:
When the form submits, `ask` stops the normal browser form navigation and checks that there is a question, a loaded walkthrough, and no answer already in progress.

It appends ‘Selected snapshot: agentic_louis/code_walk_web/app.js, lines 114–121.’ to our question. The request also contains the complete walkthrough, the current step ID, and the latest 20 conversation messages. This is how a question about one selected range still gets context from all four source files.

The handler opens the Conversation tab, disables duplicate submission, and shows a pending message.

The payload also carries the model picked below the question box. An empty value leaves model selection to the Codex default.
steps.inputs: The question, selection, current step, loaded source snapshots, and previous messages.
steps.watch_for: The selected range is embedded in the question text. It does not replace the full walkthrough or change the active step ID.

steps.title: Cross from browser to local server
steps.explanation:
The `ask` handler calls `api('/api/chat', payload)`. This shared helper serializes the payload as JSON and sends a POST request to the same local server that serves the page. It includes the server-issued token in the `X-Code-Walk-Token` header.

The function waits for a JSON response. A failed HTTP status becomes a JavaScript Error, which the caller will display in the conversation. Now follow this request into code_walk.py.
steps.inputs: The /api/chat path and the assembled payload.
steps.outputs: An HTTP request now; a parsed response or an Error later.
steps.watch_for: This adapter waits for a complete response. Model answers are not streamed into the browser token by token.

steps.title: Check the request before starting an agent
steps.explanation:
Python receives the POST in `WalkHandler.do_POST`. It checks the local request origin and token, allows only the supported routes, limits the body size, and parses a JSON object. For /api/chat it calls `chat_prompt` before taking the single available chat slot.

If another answer already occupies that slot, the server returns HTTP 429. Otherwise it calls `ask_codex`. The `finally` block ensures that the slot is released after success or failure.
steps.inputs: HTTP headers and the JSON body from app.js.
steps.outputs: A validated prompt and a call to ask_codex, or an HTTP error.
steps.watch_for: The token and local-origin checks protect this local endpoint; they are not a user-account authentication system.

steps.title: Give the agent the complete picture
steps.explanation:
Before the child process starts, `chat_prompt` validates the walkthrough, question length, conversation message roles, and active step reference. It then combines tutor instructions with the walkthrough and question as JSON data.

Our range 114–121 travels inside the question. The source text of index.html, app.js, code_walk.py, and process.py travels inside `walkthrough.files`. The agent can therefore explain how the selected JavaScript connects to the Python server. It is instructed to cite source paths and lines and to distinguish included snapshots from local changes.

The prompt also asks for structured source references with paths, verified line ranges, and short explanations. Additional files can then be attached by the server and opened from the answer.
steps.inputs: The browser payload after HTTP parsing.
steps.outputs: One prompt string for the Codex subprocess.
steps.watch_for: The walkthrough explains code as captured in its snapshots. Local files may have changed since the artifact was generated.

steps.title: Start Codex as a child process
steps.explanation:
`ask_codex` starts `codex exec` directly with an argument list. This implementation requests a read-only sandbox, disables interactive approvals, ignores user configuration, and asks for JSON Lines output. The selected repository becomes the child's working directory.

Standard input carries the prompt; standard output and error are captured. A new process session lets the timeout path stop the process group later. Before starting, Python calls `child_environment()` from process.py, which we visit next.

When a model ID is selected, the adapter adds it as a separate --model argument before starting Codex. The default leaves this argument out.
steps.inputs: The complete prompt and the repository path.
steps.outputs: A running Codex child, or a readable error if it cannot start.
steps.watch_for: A working Codex installation and authentication are still needed. This walkthrough does not invoke the child process.

steps.title: Choose what the child inherits
steps.explanation:
The cross-file call `child_environment()` copies the parent process environment but removes names beginning with `JIRA_` and the `SLACK_WORKFLOW_URL` variable. Other entries, including PATH, remain available to the child.

This returns a dictionary to the `Popen` call in code_walk.py. The browser never receives this dictionary. Once Codex starts, control returns to `ask_codex` to send the prompt and wait.
steps.inputs: The Python server's current process environment.
steps.outputs: An environment dictionary passed only to the child process.
steps.watch_for: This filters specific worker credentials; it is not a general removal of all sensitive environment variables.

steps.title: Wait for completion or a timeout
steps.explanation:
Back in code_walk.py, `communicate(prompt, timeout=180)` writes the prompt to the child and collects its output until completion. On success, execution continues to the JSON event parser in step 12.

If the 180-second wait expires, Python calls `stop_group` in process.py, then raises a short error asking for a narrower question. The next step follows only that timeout branch. A nonzero child exit status also becomes an error rather than a displayed answer.
steps.inputs: The running child and the prepared prompt.
steps.outputs: Collected output on success, or an exception on timeout or failed exit.
steps.watch_for: Cleanup can add time beyond the 180-second wait. Captured raw child errors are not sent back to the browser here.

steps.title: Timeout branch: stop the process group
steps.explanation:
This helper belongs to process.py, but the caller is the chat adapter in code_walk.py. If the child has already exited, it returns immediately. Otherwise it sends SIGTERM to the process group and waits up to ten seconds. If the group leader still has not exited, it sends SIGKILL and waits again.

On this branch, control returns to `ask_codex`, which raises the timeout error; the server eventually returns HTTP 400 and the browser displays the message. For the next step, resume the successful branch instead: Codex completed and its output is ready to parse.
steps.inputs: The subprocess object created by ask_codex.
steps.outputs: A stopped and waited-for process, followed by the caller's timeout error.
steps.watch_for: This branch does not produce a model answer. Processes that detach into other process groups may not be reached by the group signal.

steps.title: Success branch: extract the answer
steps.explanation:
Codex emits JSON Lines events about tool use and agent messages. The parser collects completed agent-message text and rejects error or failed-turn events. It returns the last completed message because earlier messages can be progress updates.

The CLI was started with --output-schema, so the final message is itself JSON containing an answer and source references. For example, the model can name the answer.schema.json file and a verified line range. Command output is not included as an answer. The next step follows this structured result back to the HTTP handler.
steps.inputs: The completed child's JSON Lines output.
steps.outputs: The final structured answer as JSON text, or a ValueError on failure.
steps.watch_for: A successful process exit alone is insufficient; the adapter also checks the event stream.

steps.title: Return from Python to the browser
steps.explanation:
The adapter returns its final JSON text to the HTTP handler, which releases the chat slot. Before sending the response, chat_result parses the answer and resolves its code references.

References to existing files use the walkthrough snapshots. For a new file, the server reads the local UTF-8 source, checks the cited range, and computes a snapshot hash. The response includes answer text, clickable references, any new file snapshots, and warnings for unavailable references.

The original fetch in app.js can now complete. Failures still become HTTP 400 responses with an error message.
steps.inputs: The adapter's answer string or exception.
steps.outputs: A JSON response with answer, references, files, statuses, and warnings, or an error.
steps.watch_for: The semaphore is released even if the model invocation fails, allowing another question afterward.

steps.title: Display the answer and allow a follow-up
steps.explanation:
After awaiting the response, attachAnswerFiles adds new source snapshots to the browser document and refreshes the file dropdown. message displays the explanation plus Related code cards. Clicking a card calls openReference, which opens its file and highlights the cited lines while preserving the current walkthrough step.

The history entry includes both the answer and its source references. Future questions carry the expanded walkthrough, and Export includes the new source snapshots. The original walkthrough file on disk is unchanged.

On a request failure the typed question is restored. The finally block always removes the pending message and enables the controls again.
steps.inputs: The parsed response or the Error thrown by api.
steps.outputs: An answer with related code cards, expanded file context, and an enabled question box.
steps.watch_for: Conversation history is kept in browser memory and is cleared when the page reloads.

glossary.definition: The data sent with the request: question, source snapshots, selected range in the question text, active step, and prior messages.
An exact copy of source text captured in the walkthrough file, with a digest used to detect local changes.
Pause this asynchronous JavaScript function until an operation completes, while the browser remains able to handle other interaction.
A shared slot that allows only one model request to run in this server at a time.
A stream of separate JSON objects, one per line. Here each object describes a Codex event.
Related operating-system processes that can receive a termination signal together during cleanup.

introduction.request: How does a question about selected code reach Codex and become an answer in the UI?
introduction.body:
Code Walk connects the code you are reading to a local, read-only agent. The browser packages your question with the selected lines, source snapshots, and conversation history. The Python server validates that context and starts Codex in the chosen repository. When Codex finishes, the server checks its code references and the browser shows the answer beside the source.

Follow one successful question through these components. The walkthrough also branches into timeout cleanup; that branch runs only when the model does not finish in time.
